transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Amy Held.
Today, flights are once again taking off from U.S. airports, but thousands still cancelled
and delayed, cascading effects from yesterday's rare four-plus-hour nationwide ground stop.
The Trump administration says outdated technology caused failures in radar and communication
systems and that there's no evidence of a cyber attack but they cannot rule it out.
A press conference is underway.
Experts say it will be days, at least, for airlines to get their operations back on track.
NPR's Eva Pukach is at Tampa International Airport today and reports on some of those
challenges for passengers.
"At my particular terminal when I'm looking up at the board right now, roughly just under
half of the flights have some sort of delay or cancellation.
I'm headed to Atlanta and even that's a mixed bag where if my flight is still on but several
around it have been cancelled.
On my way in, I also saw lots of people sleeping in chairs and just trying to get any little
bit of rest.
Some of these folks have likely been here since yesterday afternoon."
NPR's Eva Pukach.
In a Peoria, Illinois community, thousands of people had to evacuate after authorities
say they found a bomb near an ethanol plant.
Ryan Denham from member station WCBU reports, there's no word on a suspect.
Authorities say the potential one-mile blast radius from bio-urger renewables led to that
evacuation starting Friday night, including downtown Peoria.
Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon says bomb technicians rendered the package itself safe, but a full
search of the facility is underway.
"We understand that this is a disruptive process for our residents and guests.
We're asking for the public's patience while we work to make this area safe."
Shelters are set up at nearby schools and community centers.
For NPR News, I'm Ryan Denham in Peoria, Illinois.
Stocks on Wall Street gained ground this week as gas prices fell.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports all of the major indices rose more than 2 percent for the week.
Gasoline prices dipped below $4 a gallon this week for the first time in three months.
That took some of the sting out of inflation reports showing the overall cost of living
continues to climb.
Wholesale prices in October were up 6.5 percent from a year ago, the biggest annual increase
in nearly four years.
Investors expect the Federal Reserve to respond by raising interest rates next month.
Jensen Wong stepped down as CEO of the AI chip-making giant NVIDIA after acknowledging
an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
The rest of the tech sector was unscathed, however, the Nasdaq gained 2.25 percent for
the week.
Scott Horsley in PR News, Washington.
Microsoft says services are now fully restored after a massive global outage.
Today, the company announced that it had addressed the underlying technical issue, not a cyber
attack.
And you're listening to NPR News.
The most famous highway in the U.S. is celebrating 100 years.
Route 66, stretching more than 2,000 miles from Chicago to Los Angeles, has had an incalculable
effect on the American imagination.
NPR's Mandelit Delbarco takes a pop culture road trip through history.
The classic Route 66 road trip passes roadside motels, retro diners, and tourist attractions,
a quintessential American experience celebrated in song.
Get your kicks on Route 66.
Nat King Cole and his daughter Natalie both recorded versions of this song.
So did Bing Crosby, Chuck Berry, The Rolling Stones, Depeche Mode, and many others.
In the 1930s, photographer Dorothea Lange chronicled migrants along Route 66, escaping
the Dust Bowl.
Writer John Steinbeck wrote about it in his novel The Grapes of Wrath, which was made into
a film.
Route 66 has also been featured in many other movies, TV shows, music videos, and the animated
movie Cars.
Mandelit Delbarco, NPR News.
Forecasters have a message this weekend for those in the Bay Area.
Stay away from the water.
Waves of up to 50 feet could come crashing down, especially during this afternoon's
high tide.
Rainfall and winds are pushing the water that's in addition to flooding in the region as a
super El Nino warms the ocean, expanding it.
Consurfers, on the other hand, are hearing another call.
They are flocking to Mavericks Beach, south of San Francisco, hoping to ride waves as
big as buildings, a rarity, some traveling from as far away as France.
This is NPR News.
Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks?
Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News now, sponsor free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism and get NPR+ at plus.npr.org.
That's plus.npr.org.

topics.text: Flights resume at U.S. airports after yesterday's rare nationwide ground stop, with thousands still delayed or cancelled
Tampa International Airport passengers face widespread delays and cancellations; NPR's Eva Pukach reports
Thousands evacuated in Peoria, Illinois after a bomb is found near an ethanol plant; no suspect named
Wall Street stocks gain for the week as gas prices dip below $4 a gallon
October wholesale prices rise 6.5 percent from a year ago, biggest annual increase in nearly four years
Jensen Huang steps down as NVIDIA CEO after acknowledging an affair with suspected Chinese spy
Microsoft says global cloud services fully restored after massive outage, not caused by cyberattack
Route 66 marks its 100th anniversary, with NPR's Mandalit del Barco tracing its cultural history
Bay Area braces for dangerous waves up to 50 feet as super El Niño drives flooding and surfers flock to Mavericks
